 Divorce, drama and disappointment: Is “The Remarried Empress” worth the watch?
 Kristina Oang and Taylor Hwang 
 | 
 November 19, 2026 
 The drama’s main promotional photo, courtesy of @webtoonofficial on Instagram. 
 About half of marriages end in divorce. Despite this high percentage, the Eastern Empire was so shaken when Empress Navier accepted her husband’s request for divorce that it took 262 chapters and 63 side stories to cover it all. “The Remarried Empress” is a South Korean romance fantasy web novel created by Alphatart, which gained immense popularity once it was adapted into a webtoon illustrated by Sumpul. On Nov. 3, Disney+ premiered the first four episodes of a live-action adaptation directed by Cho Su-won, featuring renowned Korean actors Shin Min-a and Lee Jong-suk as the main leads. 
 The story follows Navier Trovi, the well-respected empress of the Eastern Empire, who is married to Emperor Sovieshu Vict. They were promised to each other in their youth and grew to love each other, but their relationship is destroyed when the emperor brings back a runaway slave named Rashta as his mistress, despite swearing that he would never take anyone but Navier. Rather than begging for her husband’s loyalty, Navier accepts Sovieshu’s request for divorce on one condition: that she can marry Prince Heinrey of the rival Western Kingdom. 
 K: As someone who read around 150 chapters of the webtoon out of the almost 250, I would say that the premise of the story is very interesting. However, I’m not sure how to feel about the television adaptation. I was hoping it would be more faithful to the original story, especially in the smaller details. There are many moments in the show that felt too long, to the point where I felt uncomfortable or got secondhand embarrassment from what the characters were doing (often just staring into each other’s eyes — and into my soul!).  
 Despite these moments of cringe, I will be sticking around for the final episodes to see Navier stand up to Sovieshu while the lies around Rashta unfold. We stopped at Episode 5, which covers the first 15 chapters of the webtoon. This makes me worried. If Episode 10 is meant to line up with Season 1’s ending in the webtoon (Chapter 85), the next five episodes might be too rushed or condensed. 
 T: I read part of the webtoon a long time ago, so the inaccuracies did not bother me as much. The plot does seem promising, but the lack of drama in the show bores me. I’ve watched half of the series, yet there have been no shocking scenes or even minor plot twists. I am not sure how they will fit the webtoon’s entire plot, which has 247 chapters, into 10 episodes. It is simply not enough, especially considering how slow the pacing is. Hopefully it will ramp up in the last half.  
 The first 15 minutes of episode one create the sense that this is not actually a romance story, but rather one about a strong female protagonist protecting her nation from magical threats. This occurs through a scene where Navier is chased by a worm-like creature (think of an off-brand “Dune” worm) after she splits from Sovieshu during a hunt. While it showcases the couple’s “strength” and ability to work together, the next five minutes depict Sovieshu saving Rashta from assassins/slave catchers — with 20 seconds dedicated to the two looking into each other’s eyes and romantic music playing in the background. Notably, none of this worm-chase situation happens in the original story; instead, Sovieshu finds Rashta caught in a bear trap during a hunt that Navier is not involved in. 
 The TV adaptation especially strays from the story in its styling, as characters with certain defined features in the original story lack them in the K-drama. Grand Duke Kaufman of the desert kingdom of Luipt is described as tan and with silver hair in the novel and depicted as such in the webtoon. In the live action, he is quite the opposite, with pale skin and black hair.  
 Heinrey in the show vs. webtoon, photos courtesy of @webtoonofficial on Instagram 
 The budget must not have included money for hair dye because Navier and Heinrey, who are both blond, are very not-blonde in the live action. In Heinrey’s case, his eye color is unclear in the live-action adaptation: there is a scene where Navier says that Heinrey’s eyes are purple and we see them as such, but in almost all future scenes, they are brown. 
 Styling continues to be an issue beyond story inaccuracies, with characters’ outfits not seeming to match each other in terms of time period. The world of the story seems to blend aspects of various actual time periods, but it is still mainly set in a historical empire with a high society that revolves around gossip. This sets the expectation that characters would dress in similar styles appropriate for the historical setting. Navier wears dresses with modern silhouettes, while her ladies-in-waiting and other female characters wear dresses resembling Regency-era fashion.  
 It is not just an issue for the female characters: in episode 1, Sovieshu wears an oversized light blue suit with a bedazzled lapel and no button-up underneath — just bare chest — paired with a gold necklace. While he does wear V-neck tops in the webtoon, those are styled more as casual tunics, not like the K-drama’s “headed to the club” vibe.  
 Perhaps the biggest controversy of all has been the casting. A major complaint is how inaccurate it is and how much older the actors look compared to their webtoon counterparts, with both main leads in their 40s. The series is set in a Western world, so naturally Korean actors will not resemble the drawings in the webtoon. Although the leads do look older, we find it fitting to cast more mature actors as emperor and empress. Plus, both of the main leads are renowned actors in Korea, so their appearance would draw a bigger audience.  
 According to TikTok user @thebryanjun, Koreans have been complaining that the actor for Sovieshu is “too ugly or too old,” with some even saying he should play a servant rather than a king. Harsh! Lee Jong-suk, who portrays Prince Henirey, claimed he initially rejected the role. During his Nov. 3 appearance on the YouTube talk show Salon Drip , the actor revealed that he thought Prince Heinrey’s character required a “genuinely beautiful and handsome” actor. He felt that playing Prince Heinrey would be too much pressure; he even suggested someone else take the part.  
 Although he eventually accepted the role, his hesitation illustrates how critical fans can be when an actor does not fit a character perfectly or look a certain way. Regardless of his appearance, Lee was able to pull off the Prince’s flirty and playful, yet serious personality well. 
 Recently, fans have criticized the drama’s decision to portray Rashta, a young runaway slave, as a villain. While Sovieshu is disliked for his infidelity, Rashta receives more hatred for using manipulation to climb the social hierarchy. Although her actions can be deceptive, her traumatic upbringing provides important context. The series shows her and other slaves being brutally whipped, some even to death. After escaping and being saved by Sovieshu, it is understandable that she would cling to someone who could offer her freedom. Portraying Rashta as an irredeemable villain, while also overlooking her trauma, carries classist undertones. Other characters also ridicule her lack of aristocratic manners and literacy, treating the consequences of slavery and systemic oppression as personal flaws. 
 Despite all of this, the show is still an entertaining watch. If you’re unfamiliar with the original story, this K-drama is a good pick if you’re looking for a slow romance-fantasy drama or a way to kill time instead of studying for finals. I would recommend fans of the series to check it out, but go in with low expectations for its accuracy to the web novel. If the live action was not your cup of tea, don’t worry because the anime adaptation will be released in 2027 on Crunchyroll! And who knows how else they’ll try to milk this franchise?
